title: Isoprene-emitting trees and climate response
summary: Using forest inventory data, Taylor et al. estimated the proportional abundance of isoprene-emitting trees (pIE) at 103 lowland tropical sites and quantified temporal composition shifts in three forests exposed to anomalous warming or drought. Across the landscape, pIE increased with mean annual temperature but decreased with dry-season length; through time, it increased strongly under high temperatures and more moderately following drought. The study identifies isoprene emission as a plant trait associated with species responses to climate and suggests that community selection for isoprene-emitting species may contribute to forest resilience.
uncertainty: The study combines broad landscape comparisons with temporal analyses across different forests and stressors. Isoprene emission may trade off with strategies such as leaf deciduousness, and the reported associations do not isolate a single causal mechanism or establish that isoprene alone determines resilience at San Emilio.

title: Floristic and functional change, 1976–1996
summary: The first two surveys were used to assess changes in species composition, stem abundance, and functional composition in relation to disturbance history and drought exposure.
uncertainty: The comparison is observational, and drought, succession, prior land use, and other disturbances cannot be separated as independent causes.

title: Functional composition across three surveys
summary: Three surveys spanning approximately 30 years were used to quantify population dynamics, species richness, functional diversity, and directional compositional change.
uncertainty: The study documents temporal associations; it does not assign the observed changes to a single causal mechanism.

title: Drought and canopy phenology from climate and remote sensing
summary: Climate records, long-term plot observations, Landsat data through 2017, MODIS data from 2001–2017, and other imagery were integrated to evaluate drought exposure, canopy deciduousness, wet-season greenness, and response to the 2015 ENSO drought.
uncertainty: The climate, satellite, and stem-survey records cover different periods and spatial supports. Their associations do not identify a causal effect of drought. The study reported no directional change in mean annual precipitation after 1980 and no long-term change in annual productivity during 2001–2017.

title: Published evidence through 2017
summary: Studies using the 1976–2006 plot surveys and satellite observations through 2017 report directional floristic and functional change and changes in canopy phenology. The 2019–21 census has not been included in the cited peer-reviewed analyses.
uncertainty: The studies use different temporal windows, response variables, and observation methods. The evidence is site-specific and should not be generalized to other tropical dry forests without independent tests.
source: Synthesis of Enquist and Enquist 2011, Swenson et al. 2020, and Huang et al. 2021
